directions: Plant the small tubers in humus-rich, well-drained woodland soil in dappled to full shade, ideally beneath deciduous trees that leaf out after the plant has bloomed. This dainty Japanese woodlander pushes up tiny white, anemone-like flowers with striking violet-blue anthers in very early spring, often before the last snow has melted, followed by finely dissected foliage that dies back by summer. Keep soil evenly moist through the growing and flowering season, then allow it to dry out somewhat during summer dormancy, mimicking the deciduous forest floor of its native range. It resents disturbance once established and slowly forms tight, long-lived clumps in a shaded rock garden or woodland setting.

Plant bulbs in late summer in gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun, siting them where they will bake dry through summer dormancy. Unlike its fall-blooming relatives, this Caucasus and Central Asian native sends up strap-shaped leaves in autumn and holds them through winter, then opens goblet-shaped, glossy yellow crocus-like flowers in late winter to very early spring, often before the snow has fully receded. Give it a hot, dry summer rest and avoid any supplemental irrigation once the foliage yellows in late spring, since rot in wet soil is the main cause of failure. It is best planted at the base of a warm south-facing wall or in a raised bulb frame in climates with damp summers.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in summer or early fall with the neck at or just above the soil surface; do not water during the summer dormant period before bloom.

directions: Grow exactly as you would the species: in well-drained, even dry soil in full sun, with the bulb neck left exposed at the surface. 'Hathor' is a prized pure white-flowered selection of the South African belladonna lily, producing the same leafless, late-summer flower stalks topped with a fragrant cluster of large trumpets, but in clean white rather than the typical pink. Leaves follow the flowers and persist through winter and spring before the plant goes dormant and dry through summer heat. Because it is a color selection rather than a different species, its drought tolerance, longevity, and clump-forming habit match the straight species closely, so treat plantings the same as ordinary belladonna lily beds.

common_name: Johannesburg Belladonna Lily (Deep Rose Naked Lady)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in summer or early fall with the neck at or just above the soil surface; do not water during the summer dormant period before bloom.

directions: Site and care for this selection exactly as you would ordinary belladonna lily: well-drained, even dry soil in full sun, with a hot dry summer dormancy that triggers autumn bloom. 'Johannesburg' is a named South African color form prized for its richly saturated rose-red flowers, deeper and more intensely colored than the typical soft pink species, carried in clusters atop bare stalks in late summer and early fall. Strap-like leaves emerge after flowering and persist into spring before dying back for summer rest. Give it years without disturbance in a warm, sharply drained bed, where it will bulk up into an impressive flowering clump like its species parent.

Plant the small bulbs in gritty, very sharply drained soil in full sun, ideally on a slope or raised bed, since this dainty species from the hills above Nice is far less tolerant of wet, heavy ground than its larger cousins. Slender, glaucous, grass-like leaves are topped in mid to late spring by thin wiry stems carrying small nodding white bells with a faint green tinge at the tip. It is more of a rock garden or trough plant than a border bulb, forming tidy small tufts rather than large clumps, and appreciates a dry summer rest once the foliage fades. In climates with damp summers it performs best in a bulb frame or very fast-draining scree bed.
